extracted.intended_audience: aspiring poets, literary writers, and readers of Romantic-era literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and principles for composing unified descriptive/lyrical poetry and for conducting literary study — choosing a subject that binds parts into a whole, working from immediate observation, and studying past masters. Also includes practical notes on publishing and audience risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unifying subject that supplies natural connection and unity
rubrics_metrics.description: “I sought for a subject, that should give equal room and freedom for description, incident, and impassioned reflections on men, nature, and society, yet supply in itself a natural connection to the parts, and unity to the whole.” (critical reaction to THE TASK’s defect that its title-subject was not carried beyond the first pages.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a central organising subject for a long poem that inherently links its sections so the work has natural continuity and unity; Coleridge’s proposed example is tracing a stream from source to seaport as a unifying trajectory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid awkward connections and abrupt, arbitrary transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: “the connections are frequently awkward, and the transitions abrupt and arbitrary.” (critique of THE TASK)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure transitions between parts arise logically from the subject or preceding material; avoid dropping or abandoning the nominal subject early in the work or inserting unrelated digressions that break formal unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work from immediate observation — make 'studies' in the field
rubrics_metrics.description: “With my pencil and memorandum-book in my hand, I was making studies, as the artists call them, and often moulding my thoughts into verse, with the objects and imagery immediately before my senses.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use on-site sketching and note-taking (pencil and memorandum-book) to gather concrete imagery and impressions; mould verse from objects and imagery actually perceived to strengthen descriptive vividness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select subjects that allow variety: description, incident, and impassioned reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: The desired subject should “give equal room and freedom for description, incident, and impassioned reflections on men, nature, and society.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing a theme for an extended poem, prefer subjects that naturally accommodate multiple modes (scenic description, narrative incident, and moral/philosophical reflection) so the poem can be rich and varied without losing coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study past masters and historical/language sources closely
rubrics_metrics.description: Coleridge recounts reading the Minnesinger, Hans Sachs, Pindar, Chaucer, Dante, Milton and labouring “through sufficient specimens of the master singers” and learning German and Gothic sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read widely and with attention to language and historical forms; study the works and techniques of canonical poets and older traditions (including in original or careful translations) to inform craft and vocabulary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground persuasive or argumentative prose in principles for durability
rubrics_metrics.description: On Burke: “He referred habitually to principles. He was a scientific statesman; and therefore a seer. For every principle contains in itself the germs of a prophecy...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In essays or persuasive writing, appeal to underlying principles rather than transient details or partisan rhetoric; principle-grounded argumenting tends to age better and retain interest beyond the immediate moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about offensive or ill-judged religious/political applications in periodicals
rubrics_metrics.description: “In the second number an essay against fast days, with a most censurable application of a text from Isaiah for its motto, lost me near five hundred of my subscribers at one blow.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know your readership and the medium: provocative or insensitive use of religious texts or unexpected polemics in a serial publication can alienate subscribers and damage readership; measure risks of topical dissent in the chosen forum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical expectation: literature is not a reliable profession for many
rubrics_metrics.description: “I saw plainly, that literature was not a profession, by which I could expect to live; for I could not disguise from myself... that whatever my talents might or might not be in other respects, yet they were not of the sort that could enable me to become a popular writer.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat writing as uncertain income; consider supplemental work (e.g., verses for newspapers, patrons) and realistic expectations about popularity and financial return when planning a literary career.
